meta.title: Vietnamese A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Vietnamese → English (see the Vietnamese, recall the meaning) and English → Vietnamese (see an English meaning, recall the Vietnamese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Vietnam's own framework for learners of Vietnamese publishes no graded word list, and neither does any exam board, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 269 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — relatives and the people around you, jobs and the workplace, school and study, clothes and shopping, more food, cooking and the market, the furniture of a home, the town and its places, the countryside and animals, the seasons and the points of the compass, travel and directions, health and the body, feelings and character, free time, sport and festivals such as Tết, telling what happened and when, giving an opinion, more classifiers, and the everyday verbs of moving, dressing and doing — and the other 481 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Vietnamese, counted in film and television subtitles. Vietnamese writes a space between syllables rather than between words, so the subtitles were divided into words against the dictionary first, and a two-syllable word such as học sinh (pupil) is counted as one word. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Beneath every headword its tones are named, one per syllable — ngang (no mark), huyền (à), sắc (á), hỏi (ả), ngã (ã) and nặng (ạ) — read off the marks the word is spelt with. 123 nouns show their classifier, the word that stands between a number and the noun (hai con mèo, two cats), and 275 words borrowed from Chinese show the characters they come from. The pronunciation is given in IPA for Hanoi and, where it differs, for Saigon. Real example sentences come with 732 of the 750 words, three apiece for 703 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Spellings are Wiktionary's, which often puts the tone mark in the older place (hoà, khoẻ); the newer (hòa, khỏe) is equally correct. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, classifiers, characters and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the OpenSubtitles 2018 Vietnamese text (opensubtitles.org, via the OPUS corpus collection), counted here. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
